maintopic: KING ALBERT OF BELGIUM
KING ALBERT OF BELGIUM
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY-EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: KING ALBERT OF BELGIUM
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY-EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be the
sense of this house that we should place on record our very deep sympathy with the Belgian people in the loss they have suffered through the sudden and unexpected death of their sovereign, and that we should extend also our deepest sympathy to the bereaved family.
In the end of July and the beginning of August, 1914, the late King of the Belgians was the well-beloved monarch of a small nation with a relatively limited population. Within a month he had become one of the great figures of the world. If one were to ask how this came about, the answer, I think, would be found in the character of the man.
King Albert of Belgium

who at that moment was sovereign of the Belgian people. The neutrality of his country had been guaranteed by treaty. When Germany determined to march against France the plan of campaign, as prepared by her military leaders, contemplated crossing Belgian soil. That was a violation of neutrality. It is difficult at this time to determine just what discussions took place and to what extent conciliatory efforts were used for the purpose of inducing those in authority in Belgium to consent to such action. But out of all the confusion and doubt on that question there emerges one clear-cut fact, and that is that the King of the Belgians was prepared to sacrifice everything except honour in defence of his people and of the integrity of his kingdom. From that moment on he became a world figure. He must have realized, as everyone did, that that small nation could not resist the onslaught of the great moving millions of Germany, and when his cities fell one after the other, when his country became almost a dependency of a foreign country and governed by a foe, as it was for so many years, he still pursued his course at the head of 'his army, sharing in their vicissitudes their losses and their gains. In the end he was privileged as the head not only of his own armies but of the armies of the north of France and of some British troops, the cavalry brigade of Canada and some detached engineering and railway units, to march back into his kingdom and repossess it.
His place in history is assured. The suddenness of his death and the circumstances attending it will add lustre to the glory of his name. We, far-removed from his kindgom, perhaps do not realize the extent to which he had become beloved by his people. Democratic, and yet in every sense a king, he and his queen had so endeared themselves to their people that I fancy few more popular sovereigns ever sat upon a throne. We Canadians were not closely in contact with the operations which he directed until the end when he repossessed himself of his kingdom, but I think we can share, as our troops shared under the command which he had over his own and the British and Canadian forces at the end, the sorrow of his people and extend the sympathy which Canadians have for those who have lost a heroic sovereign, one whose courage and determination have given him a place among the heroic figures of the world. In that sense I am sure that this House of Commons and the parliament of Canada will join with all the peoples of the world who honour and respect courage, bravery and the qualities that make for enduring fame among

the citizens of the world, in extending our sympathy to the bereaved royal family and people of Belgium in the great loss which they have sustained.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: KING ALBERT OF BELGIUM
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY-EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
As leader of
the official opposition in this House of Commons, I deem it a privilege to join with the right lion, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in the sentiments which he has expressed on behalf of the Canadian people in appreciation of the truly great and noble life of the late King Albert I of Belgium; and of the loss which Belgium and the world has sustained in the late king's sudden and tragic death.
I join as well, on behalf of hon. members on this side of the house, with the Prime Minister and hon. members on the government side, in the sympathy which the Prime Minister has expressed with Her Majesty the Queen of Belgium, and the members of the Belgian royal family, in their personal bereavement, and with the people of Belgium in their national loss.
Character, and the circumstances of his time, combined to give to the late king most of the attributes of the mythical hero of legendary days. It is in no way due to convention that in all parts of the world to-day, King Albert of Belgium's many virtues as a sovereign and as a man are being extolled. He, if ever monarch was, will be remembered as a Knight of the Holy Grail; a man who found the joy and fullness of life in high and noble adventure. The manner of his death portrayed the quest of his soul.
The world, in these days of anxiety and uncertainty, will greatly mourn the loss of one whose personality and patriotism did so much to unite the crown and the people in bonds of mutual confidence and affection. It will, however, recognize as a legacy to all mankind, what it now recalls of Albert's kingly and heroic leadership of his country in time of peril; his rigid regard at all times, as a sovereign, for constitutional practice and procedure; his never-failing solicitude for the well-being of his subjects; his democratic sympathies and behaviour; and his exemplary personal life.

maintopic: KING ALBERT OF BELGIUM
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY-EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, King Albert of Belgium whose death we mourn to-day was beloved by his subjects and revered the world over for his great and sterling qualities. May I be permitted to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in expressing to the royal family and the people of Belgium our sincere sympathy in their irreparable loss.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient, in view of the large amounts of money invested by the dominion in canals and railroads, that all goods shipped through the canals owned and operated by the Government of Canada be subject to taxation.
He said: The motion standing on the order paper in my name, which you have just read, Mr. Speaker, is one I shall discuss for a few minutes this afternoon from the standpoint of finance and present-day business and transportation. It is not my intention to ask this country or this government to do anything contrary to the usual practice of the nations of the world to-day; that, I think, would be impossible. The seas are the common highway of mankind; on them there are no preferred claims, no prescriptive rights. And what pertains to the seas pertains also, to a lesser degree, to the navigable streams of this or any other country. When nature has placed impediments that have to be circumvented or removed by man and these obstructions are overcome it is a recognized fact that countries incurring that expense are entitled to collect tolls to reimburse them for their outlay. But I think it is also a generally recognized international practice that there must be no discrimination between

Water Transportation-Mr. McGibbon
countries. That was first laid down, in a treaty between Great Britain and the United States in 1850, the Clayton-Bulwer treaty. It was reiterated in the Washington treaty of 1870 and again in the convention of Constantinople which regulated tolls on the Suez canal. The principle was again recognized in the Hay-Pauncefote treaty of 1901 and lastly in the treaty signed at Washington in 1910 between Canada and the United States. Nearly all these treaties carry similar clauses. As the Clayton-Bulwer treaty was superseded by the Hay-Pauncefote treaty we can pass that over. But we find in the convention of Constantinople, which was signed by Great Britain, Russia, France, Spain, Italy and Germany, the following clause regarding the Suez canal:
The Suez maritime canal shall always be free and open in time of war as in time of peace to every vessel of commerce or war without distinction of flag.
That again was copied almost word for word in the Hay-Pauncefote treaty of 1901 and a similar idea is expressed in the Washington treaty and the treaty of 1910 in connection with the international boundary waters of Canada and the United States. Consequently, I do not think it would be wise, as so many journals and some individuals in Canada are suggesting to-day, to discriminate either for or against any other country, but rather, we should exercise our rights as they are being exercised by other nations and levy on the tonnage going through our canals a sufficient tax to recompense us, at least in part, for the great expenditures we have made.
In this day and generation it is a fair maxim that every service which is costing the country a considerable sum of money should bring us some return. If we stop for a moment to look at the vast sums of money that we have tied up in our water transportation systems I think the house and the country will agree with me that the dominion should get some return. We have some $245,000,000 invested in canals, $280,000,000 invested in wharves and harbours and, as nearly as I can find out, something over $100,000,000 invested in elevators through harbour commissions and such-like. In addition to that, we have spent some $30,000,000 or $35,000,000 in dredging the St. Lawrence river. It may be a surprise to the house to know that the return to the public treasury on this vast sum of $600,000,000 or $700,000,000 is practically nothing. If you take this sum and compound the interest at, say four per cent from the time of the investment, the total amount involved would simply stagger the country.
The time has come when we should levy on the tonnage passing through these waterways a tax that would bring at least some revenue back to the public treasury. It seems almost incomprehensible that a country owning a railway in which we have invested some $2,600,000,000, would build a water transportation system in competition with it for some 1,426 miles and run it absolutely free to every nation in the world. But that is what we have done. We make the railways build their tracks, buy their equipment, construct their terminals and operate them; then in competition we put a free waterway transportation system costing us the gross sum of $600,000,000 or $700,000,000. More than that, incredible as it may seem, every province is spending hundreds of millions of dollars on highways in competition with our railways. Ontario alone has spent $406,000,000 on highways and gravelled roads; Quebec has spent $158,000,000 in the same way, and as I have said, we have invested between $600,000,000 and $700,000,000 on a waterway system which we have made free; the highways are practically free and yet we expect our two great railway systems to meet competition of that kind and earn their expenses and some return on their investment. The whole thing is incredible.
What has been the result? Let me give just a few instances. I was raised in the county of Lambton and ore from Duluth used to come down to Point Edward in that county, being reshipped from there over the national railways to Hamilton where it was used. During the two years preceding the opening of the Welland canal more than 1,000,006 tons of ore were carried to Point Edward and on that carriage the railway received more than half a million dollars. To-day every ton of that business is lost to the railroad; the ore is now carried by United States vessels from Duluth to Hamilton. The net result is that Canada is simply bonusing United States ships to come in and take business away from our own railway.
Flour transportation from Port Arthur and Fort William is in the same position. Previously, that flour was ground and shipped to Port McNicoll and Point Edward. Since the Welland canal has been opened I am informed that the railways have lost business amounting to $1,250,000 per annum, that tonnage being nearly all carried by boats and one-third of those being foreign. Last year tonnage to the amount of 9,000,000 tons went through the Welland canal and over one-third of it was carried by ships built in foreign countries by foreign workmen and manned by foreign
702	COMMONS
Water Transportation-Mr. McOibbon
sailors. We build a waterway transportation system and give it to them free, asking them to come in and compete against our own railway transportation systems.
Take the coal that comes into Toronto. For many years that came in over our railway systems. To-day it comes in by water and the two railways are now losing more than $1,000,000 of business per annum. That has also gone partly to foreign ships. Two years ago 90,000 tons of pulpwood from Norway was carried in free through our canals, thus helping to depress the product of our own industries in the markets of Canada and the United States. That is part of the result of allowing free transportation over our waterways.
There is no doubt that the government has power to impose tolls. I could refer the house to the different treaties which I have read and which give us that power. There is a Canadian statute in which that is set out, but the greatest proof of all is that we did impose tolls and they were not abolished until 1905. I have under my hand the order in council passed in June, 1905, but as no reasons are given for the abolition of tolls, we must assume what those reasons were. But whatever the reasons were in 1905, they no longer exist. A great deal of water has gone under the bridge since then. At that time Canada had an interest bill of only $7,000,000 on its funded debt; to-day we have an interest bill of $134,000,000. The national debt was then somewhere under $300,000,000, whereas to-day it is $2,600,000,000 or $2,700,000,000. At that time we did not have a great railway system on our hands with a debt of $2,600,000,000 and this is costing and going to cost us from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000 per annum for at least the lifetime of any person in this house. We then did not have to pay $42,000,000 annually in pensions as a result of the great war, nor did we have $130,000,000 invested in the Welland canal. This colossal debt has all been piled up since that time and yet we continue to give free transportation over our inland waterways to all the ships in the world. Every other major canal that I have read anything about has tolls. Tolls are charged on the Panama canal, I saw this morning that last year they amounted to $23,000,000. That is over five per cent of the cost, which was $400,000,000. Last year one third as much tonnage went from Canada through the Panama canal as went through the Welland canal, and on goods going from and coming to Canada we paid over $3,000,000 in tolls to the Panama canal. Yet on the northern side of the United States we let an equal quantity of goods go through our canals for nothing.
[Mr. McGibbon.l
It is an asinine policy in my opinion, especially for a young country so loaded with debt as we are.
Some may differ from me, but I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this house, that the greatest transportation systems that we ever had and must have in the future are our railways. Confederation would not have been possible had we not been able to carry out the agreement to join the provinces by railway. The railways have been the great instrument of colonization, and we must preserve them. When the Duff commission made its report the railways of Canada gave employment to 163,000 people. They pay in taxes to the different treasuries of this country something over $8,000,000 per year. The canals pay nothing; there are no fees outside of the elevator charges, practically everything that is represented in the total investment is free.
Besides that, sir, this country is spending hundreds of millions on roads, and they are practically free. And now we have started in the air, and have spent some $3,000,000 on that. I think it is only fair that all the services of this country should pay a fair return on the capital invested. We have on the Welland1 canal alone a loss of about $14,-. 000,000 a year, including interest and amortization. We are spending in actual services and wages over $3,000,000 a year and not charging even that to the traffic.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a good deal of interest to the presentation of his case by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon). While he gave us a great deal of information I find that I cannot come to the conclusion that I should support his motion.

The tolls on Canadian canals were abolished I understand in 1904 or 1905, and as far as I can gather, it was done for the purpose of increasing traffic through our canals, and also because of the preponderance of American tonnage that was passing through them. That condition has been corrected in time, as was stated by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. The Canadian tonnage is now much ahead of the American, and the tonnage passing through the canals has increased very materially.
As far as I can gather there is nothing in the treaties that have been made with the United States to prevent tolls being levied. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Both-well) has quoted the treaty of 1871. I should like to quote article 1 of the waterways treaty of 1909, approved by this house in 1911. It reads:
The high contracting parties agree that the navigation of all navigable boundary waters shall for ever continue free and open for the purposes of commerce to the inhabitants and to the ships, vessels, and boats of both countries equally, subject, however, to any laws and regulations of either country, within its own territory, not inconsistent with such privilege of free navigation, and applying equally and without discrimination to the inhabitants, ships, vessels, and boats of both countries.
It is further agreed that so long as this treaty shall remain in force this same right of navigation shall extend to the waters of lake Michigan, and to all canals connecting boundary waters and now existing or which may hereafter be constructed on either side of the line. Either of the high contracting parties may adopt rules and regulations governing the use of such canals within its own territory, and may charge tolls for the use thereof; but all such rules and regulations and all tolls charged shall apply alike to the subjects or citizens of the high contracting parties and the ships, vessels, and boats of both of the high contracting parties, and they shall be placed on terms of equality in the use thereof.
That treaty was to exist for five years, after which it was to be subject to termination upon tw'elve months' notice. In the St. Lawrence deep waterway treaty which was negotiated in 1932, subject to approval by the United States governing bodies and by this parliament, there is a clause which deals with the matter to which I have just referred. Article 7 reads;
The high contracting parties agree that the rights of navigation accorded under the provisions of existing treaties between His Majesty and the United States of America shall lie maintained, notwithstanding the provisions for termination contained in any of such treaties, and declare that these treaties confer upon the subjects or citizens and upon the ships, vessels and boats of each high con-

Water Transportation-Mr. Turnbull
tracting parly, rights of navigation in the St. Lawrence river, and the great lakes system, including the canals now existing or which may hereafter be constructed.
That article has the effect of making the arrangement perpetual in character. In view of the fact that this treaty is now being discussed in the United States, I think that this resolution is rather ill-timed. I do not think we should do anything either to promote or hinder the passage of this measure in the United States. If it should pass there, well and good, it will then come to us.
Equality of treatment for the people and shipping of the United States and the people of Canada is insisted upon in the treaties of 1871, 1909 and the one now under discussion. Should Canada levy tolls without coming to an arrangement with the United States, I think it would have the effect of driving tonnage away from the Canadian canals. If that should occur the estimated revenue from these tolls will be much smaller. It will have the additional effect of increasing the cost of transportation. Hitherto our efforts have been in the direction of cheapening transportation as much as possible, especially through the canals of the St. Lawrence and the great lakes where so much wheat is transported. It is my opinion that this added cost of transportation ultimately will find its way back to the producers of wheat. If tolls are levied it will have the effect of driving business to other channels. There would be the competition of the Hudson Bay railway, the Vancouver outlet to Europe through the Panama canal and the Buffalo and Albany which is used to some extent. There would be also the Mississippi route to the gulf. These would all affect the amount of tonnage which would pass through our canals.
The speaker referred to the railroads but he did not tell the house the amount of land grants which have been made nor the subsidies paid for construction. I cannot see that the railroads have much complaint with regard to their treatment. It seems to me that in view of the fact that, transportation charges will be increased on a vital product of central Canada, the best thing we can do is to leave our canals free of tolls.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of taking up much time in discussing this interesting and important motion but I desire merely to place on record my concurrence in the views of the hon. members who have just spoken, that it would not be a proper step to take to impose an additional tax upon the water borne traffic of our internal canals. As far as western 74726-45 i
wheat is concerned the effect would be to force more wheat through Vancouver and the Panama canal. This wheat would pay tolls to the Panama canal rather than to the Canadian canals, and much of our wheat now moves in that direction.
Wheat is not the only product involved. There are large cargoes moving through our canals both east and west of lumber, ore, steel and manufactured products. Central Canada is unfortunately situated as far as access to ocean ports is concerned. It is situated far inland and produces a particular commodity in large quantities. In order that this commodity may meet the competition on the markets of the world it is necessary that transportation rates to those markets shall be as low as possible. This applies not only to the outgoing traffic consisting of wheat, cattle, meat, butter and eggs but also to the incoming traffic from eastern Canada. It is desirable that central Canada should have cheap transportation to the markets of the world as well as cheap freight rates on those things which are required to maintain production.
If a tax upon canal tolls were to favour the railroads it would have to be very high indeed. The rail rate on wheat from Fort William to Montreal is something over thirty cents per hundredweight while in normal years the water rate is something like seven or eight cents per hundredweight. In order to be of any benefit to the railroads, a tremendous tax would have to be imposed. This would be necessary before there could be anything like competition with the canals in the carriage of this particular product. Perhaps not so great a tax would be necessary in the case of other commodities, but the life of the country depends upon its ability to sell sufficient goods in order to meet its obligations in other lands and its ability to export depends upon transportation as much as upon anything else.
A tax of even one cent per bushel upon western wheat would reduce to that extent the purchasing power of the people of the prairies. To the extent that their purchasing power was reduced, the industries of eastern Canada would suffer. There would be a slowing up of the whole internal trade between the east and the west.
I do not think the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) was really in earnest when he suggested that with the $10,000,000 to be derived by this tax on canals we could afford to abolish the sugar tax. Perhaps this tax is not the most popular one in the world and I do not know of any other tax that I would be as willing to abolish. But there is this about it. The necessities of the
708	COMMONS
Water Transportation-Mr. Arthurs
case, relief and matters of that kind, made essential the gathering of revenue from new sources, and I am rather of the opinion that the amount gathered from the people in the sugar tax was more than paid back to them by extraordinary government assistance. But to place a toll on canal traffic as a substitute for the sugar tax would, to my mind, transfer the tax which is now spread over the whole of Canada to a very large extent to the two million people who reside between the Rocky mountains and the head of the great lakes, and for that reason if for no other I would oppose it.
I do not think that the imposition of such a tax as is proposed would be of any assistance to the railways. It would work a great injury to the primary products of the country, not only wheat, but lumber, ore and mineral products, in the search for markets east and west, and would also be injurious to the manufacturing industries of Canada which have to find markets, to a certain extent at least, in western Canada, over long distances of transportation. So that the whole effect of the ten millions which would be gained by that tax would be' lost through the reduction in business which it would cause, and by reducing business it would thereby reduce the tax basis of our whole system. For that reason, as well as for the reasons advanced by other lion, members, I shall have to oppose it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext:
I am not entirely in accord with the resolution, but at the same time there are a great many people in Canada who feel that they have been taxed to an inordinate degree for the support and maintenance of our canal system. I believe that the proper solution would be perhaps to place a very small tax, say a cent a ton, upon the vessels passing through these canals, or a graduated tax as the case may be, which could be worked out satisfactorily, and which would pay for the maintenance and operation of the canal system. The canal system in Canada has been largely paid for in the past. It has been written off the books of Canada, and is regarded as an asset, but we continue to pay large sums every year for the upkeep of the canals. I do not know the exact amount, but a reference to the public accounts will show how much we pay annually. It is the custom at the present time for the United States to charge a toll for vessels passing through the Panama canal, either loaded or empty.
I agree with the last speaker (Mr. Turnbull) that no tax should be placed upon the commodities raised in the west for export purposes. But I also believe that any canal, such

as the Trent canal, which has cost the country millions of dollars and which at the present time entails a very large upkeep cost, being almost entirely, if not entirely used by tourists, should make a charge on these vessels to recompense Canada for the expense involved in the maintenance of the canal. This would apply to all canals.
A tax such as I suggest, one cent a ton on vessels passing through, let us say the Welland canal, which runs through the home of my hon. friend to my left, would not embarrass the vessels. It would not increase the cost of transportation, but in a marked degree would relieve Canada of the expense of upkeep and the incidental expenses of operating these canals. I do not know that I have anything further to add. I simply wish to convey my impression to other members of the house, but I believe that something of this kind should be done. I might also add that we are not breaking any treaty with the United States. We have a treaty with that country signed in 1871, which guaranteed equal rights to American vessels passing through our canals, and providing that any tolls placed on the vessels of either country should be paid by both-that is to say, no discrimination should be made as between vessels of the United States and ours. But when we find tramp vessels coming from Norway or from other foreign countries and passing through our canals, it is perfectly right that they should pay the same tolls as they would pay in their own countries in similar circumstances.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext:
The proposition made by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) and the arguments he has used in support of his motion might seem at first glance to be entirely fair and reasonable, but one has to take into account not only the situation as it appears from a theoretical point of view but the actual facts that confront us to-day. The statement which has been made by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) sets forth clearly the situation as it appears to us from the point of view of the western provinces. Certainly the time is most inopportune to place any extra burden on the producers of wheat. Any increase in the freight rate even by the fraction of a cent must of necessity be reflected back to the producer of wheat.
Perhaps the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has over-estimated the effect upon the revenue. Let us take this fact into consideration. At the present time large quantities of wheat go via British Columbia ports and the Panama canal. There is a line drawn some-

Water Transportation-Mr. Brown
where north and south through the western prairies which would determine the route taken by the wheat. It will take the cheapest route, whatever that may be. Might I suggest that the possible effect of making the eastern route more expensive would be simply to draw that line further east and send a larger quantity of wheat via Vancouver and Prince Rupert-that I would not object to-but also via the Panama canal, to the increase of the revenues of the Panama canal and the decrease in the revenues of the transportation systems here that carry our wheat east. That is a point of view that was not considered by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario.
When a tax, even a small tax, is imposed, it often has effects that are entirely unintended and unforeseen. That is one of the things we frequently meet in our tariff taxation, and the same is true of any tax-the effect is very often different from what was intended.
I do not know that it is necessary for me at further length to register my objections to this resolution. The hon. member for Swift Current seems to me to have placed the matter before us quite adequately. Certainly the time is very inopportune to impose any extra burden upon the wheat producers of the prairie provinces.

after all, the deepening of the St. Lawrence river east of Montreal is in the same category as the canals. Does the hon. gentleman intend to impose a tax for the use of that?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext:
I have listened with a
good deal of interest to the whole discussion here this afternoon, but I have noticed that from all sides of the house and from all sections of the country opposition has come to the proposal of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon), whom I should like to congratulate on the careful and reasonable manner in which he dealt with this question. At the same time I am, to a large extent at any rate, in a similar position to those from various sections who have spoken before me in opposition to the imposition of tolls, without at least a great deal more consideration than I have been able to give to the question or without more cogent reasons being put forward than have so far been advanced by various writers and speakers. There is no doubt that the whole proposition appears attractive to some who give it more or less superficial thought, but as a matter of fact, when the question is studied there enters into it matters of international differences, injury to the grain trade of the west and complications of various kinds that make it not so attractive as it at first appears.
May I review briefly-and in this regard I shall follow the example of the other hon. members who have spoken-the whole question as it appears to me? I had intended to quote a few of the treaties that have been referred to, but as they have already been quoted from, I shall quote merely one of them, namely, the treaty of 1909, and I do this, not because it has not already been quoted-the hon. member for London (Mr. White) quoted it a few minutes ago-but simply in order to utilize it in my remarks as part of my argument. I am quoting from article one of the treaty of 1909 between Great Britain and the United States:
It is further agreed that so long as this treaty shall remain in force, this same right of navigation shall extend to the waters of lake Michigan and to all canals connecting boundary waters, and now existing or which may hereafter be constructed on either side of the line. Either of the high contracting parties may adopt rules and regulations governing the use of such canals within its own territory, and may charge tolls for the use thereof, but all such rules and regulations and all tolls charged shall apply alike to the subjects or citizens of the high contracting parties and the ships, vessels, and boats of both of the high contracting parties, and they shall be placed on terms of equality in the use thereof.
That, without doubt, confirms the other treaties such as the Webster-Ashburton treaty and the treaty of Washington of 1871, in. making the imposition of tolls, if they should) be imposed, uniform as to the United States-and Canada. The hon. member for Muskoka, in his remarks, agreed with that. The question, however, is deeper than that, because if you undertook to impose tolls on merely some of what are called foreign vessels, that is vessels outside the British Empire and, if you like, outside the United States, you would obtain so little in return that it would be of no importance to the revenues. It is apparent that if you do anything, you must do it; without discrimination of any kind; you must do it towards all the different countries that make use of the canals. I believe that principle is generally accepted, unless you wish to stir up a spirit of antagonism or economic reprisals of one kind or another, and it seems to me there is enough economic nationalism throughout the world to-day without trying to increase it.
May I give very briefly the history of canal tolls? They were established in 1873 on Canadian canals, although the United stales canal at Sault Ste. Marie remained

Water Transportation-Mr. Manion
free as did, so far as tolls were concerned, the Brie canal at that time. Therefore, as a result of the establishment of tolls on Canadian canals, Canadian grain was at that time diverted to United States ports and in 1892 the government of the day passed an order in council reducing the tolls on grain from the then rate of twenty cents to two cents per ton provided the grain went out via Canadian ports. The United States retaliated by imposing a toll of twenty cents a ton on our Canadian grain passing through the United States canal at the Soo. At that time there was no Canadian canal at Sault Ste. Marie. In consequence, in 1893, Canada did away with the preferential toll and imposed a reduced uniform toll of ten cents a ton on traffic through the Welland and St. Lawrence canals, regardless of destination. This toll was in force for the next ten years when as a result of petitions from all over Canada to the government of the day serious consideration was given the question of abolishing tolls altogether. I have under my hand a list of the organizations and public bodies which sent in petitions and for the sake of the record it might be well to name some of the different organizations that sent them. I have before me a copy of one dated March 30, 1903, from Kingston, but among those sending in petitions at that time to do away with the tolls were such bodies as these:
Montreal Corn Exchange Association.
Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.
Montreal Board of Trade.
Kingston Board of Trade.
Council of the Corporation of the City of Kingston.
Canadian Merchant Marine Association.
Toronto Board of Trade.
Calgary Board of Trade.
Kasio Board of Trade.
Sorel Board of Trade.
Owen Sound Board of Trade.
National Association of Marine Engineers of Canada.
Board of Trade of City of Ottawa.
Winnipeg Board of Trade.
Winnipeg Grain and Produce Association.
That is a list of some of the bodies which sent in petitions against the continuance of tolls. As a result, on April 27, 1903, the tolls were suspended temporarily by order in council and two years later, in 1905, the tolls were definitely abandoned. In 1902, the last year in which tolls existed, the Welland ship canal carried 646,000 tons of traffic, whereas in the next year when the tolls were abandoned, the the traffic increased to 979,000 tons, or an increase of about 50 per cent. I may add, without giving the figures, that the traffic on the St. Lawrence canals at that time also Increased by 50 per cent. It is understood
'Mr. Manior.l
of course that traffic passing through both the Welland and St. Lawrence canals paid tolls on only one canal and that would be the case if tolls were again instituted. A boat that went through the Welland canal could not be charged tolls again on going through the St. Lawrence and vice versa. To demonstrate the increase in traffic in past years I may say that in 1933 on the Welland canal the traffic carried amounted to 9,194,000 tons.
As to the earnings from those tolls, at the time they were charged, the rate on grain was ten cents a ton whether it went through the Welland or the St. Lawrence canals. Between 1893 and 1902 when tolls were being charged, the annual revenue amounted in round figures to 8230,000. I had some officials in my department take the tolls as they were in force between 1893 and 1902 and apply them to the traffic of 1932. The figures are taken not for last year but for the year before because we had more complete returns. Instead of 8230,000, the return for 1932, had we charged on the same basis as in the period from 1893 to 1902, when tolls were in force, would have been 81,480,000. Against that is the cost of operation and repairs of the canals on the through route which, in the same year, 1932, amounted to 81,634,000. Therefore I must confess that the hon. member for Muskoka was in error so far as I can find out-and I think my figures are correct- in regard to his statement that the annual charges on the Welland canal were $14,000,000. I sent out to get them in order to check myself up and I find that the charges on the Welland canal in 1932 were $738,000 or, with a few extras, nearly $739,000, about half being operation and the other half repairs. Of course, if you added the interest on the investment you would still have only about one half the figure which I think was given by my hon. friend, because the interest on the investment in the Welland canal of, as he said, $130,000,000, would probably amount to something like 87,000,000, and the cost of operation and upkeep 8738,000.
In regard to the capital investment, it is true we use immense figures in speaking of the cost of the different canals in this country. If you go back perhaps one hundred years to the building of the first canal in Canada and add all the expenditures together since then, without interest, it does come to a figure of 8245,000,000. But as a matter of fact that is hardly a fair computation, because certain of the canals have been superseded or replaced.
Suppose tolls were put on the Canadian canals, the result to my mind would be merely

Water Transportation-Mr. Manion
to drive the traffic to other routes. It would injure the eastern Canadian ports to the advantage of other parts; it would drive the traffic from Montreal, Quebec and Sorel to Churchill, if you will, or to Vancouver and the Panama canal, or by the Erie canal to New York. And as over 70 per cent of the traffic through the port of Montreal is grain it would certainly injure the port of Montreal. The average rate on grain from Port Col-borne to Montreal between 1925 and 1931 was just under 6 cents, or 5-66 cents a bushel. From Buffalo to New York it was 4-84 cents a bushel. So you would merely add to that differential and drive some of the grain traffic probably through the Erie canal, some to the Panama canal, and, as my hon. friend who just sat down said, move further east the line beyond which the grain goes west. The result would be to divert the grain; otherwise as far as I can see it would not have any particular effect. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said that at the present time one-third of the traffic of Canada goes by way of the Panama canal, I presume he means the grain traffic. So that you would merely increase the proportion of grain traffic going by the Panama canal if tolls were put on our canals; you would prevent the grain coming east and would drive it west. The statement that we could raise 810,000,000 per annum by tolls on the canals I think is extreme, in that to produce any such sum you would have to have a rate of something over $1 a ton.

speechtext: If I may correct that, it has been misquoted two or three times. I said that on last year's tonnage at Panama canal rates it would amount to that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext:
I do not dispute that. But I point out that it would require a rate of over 81 a ton. I believe the Panama canal rates are about 81.20. One dollar a ton would mean an extra charge of 3 or 4 cents a bushel on wheat. Notwithstanding anything I have heard or read I believe that impost would be against the farmers of western Canada, and I entirely agree with those from the west who say that the western Canadian grain grower cannot stand that toll added to his present cost, because the price of grain is fixed in the Liverpool market, and the cost of delivering it there is a factor affecting the Canadian farmer.
Concerning the railways, a great deal has been written in the press and stated by some speakers about the advantage that would result to the railways from charging tolls on the canals. Someone I think quoted what the Duff commission said on that point. I am
going to quote one clause at any rate. The Duff commission made this statement about the canals competing with the railways:
While on first consideration it might appear that the construction of canals which are free of all tolls to water carriers is in effect a form of state subsidy to a rival transport agency, yet in so far at least as bulk traffic in grain and heavy commodities is concerned, complaint is not made by the railways on this score. The imposition of tolls would not help and would probably hinder the railways as tending to discourage production.
And further on:
Water-borne traffic will continue to be a factor of major importance in Canadian transportation both on the inland waterways and coastwise through the Panama canal, but rail traffic in the main has been adjusted to the conditions now' existing and it does not seem probable that the developments now under way and in contemplation in connection with the Hudson's Bay route, and' the deepening of the St. Lawn'ence-great lakes canals, will seriously prejudice the "position of the railways in the future. The competition of water-borne traffic has not been an important factor in bringing about the present difficulties of the railways.
I could if I took the time quote from some railwaymen, notably the late Sir Henry Thornton, and I think Mr. Beatty also, statements showing that they were not very strongly, at any rate, of the opinion that the canals were interfering with the railways.

If the minister will permit
a question, he mentioned the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. Does he seriously contend that that would not affect the railways?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
If I said that I did not
mean to. I was speaking of the canals.
Speaking further of the railways, I wish to submit that it is not fair to say the canals have been built at public expense and the railways at private expense, as some writers have, because the railways of Canada have been very heavily subsidized. The Canadian National Railways last year required from this house 861,000,000, and it costs to operate the canals as a whole about 81,500,000 a year. We have given to the Canadian National at various times loans amounting to nearly $700,000,000, that is three times the cost of the canals, and in addition there is the interest on that money, none of which has ever been paid, and which has amounted to nearly $400,000,000. Besides that you have the cost of building the Intercolonial, the Prince Edward Island railway and the National transcontinental, amounting to another $400,000,000, upon which again nothing has ever been paid in the way of interest. And still further, you have the Maritime Freight Rates Act, by

Water Transportation-Mr. Manion
which a 20 per cent reduction in freight that is granted and reimbursed to both the Canadian National and the private railway system. There is also the deficit in operation of the eastern lines, and the $7,000,000 expended on the Prince Edward Island car ferry service. [ point these things out merely to emphasize the fact that any tolls that could be collected on the canals would be a very small contribution towards meeting the railway deficits. The railways have cost the Dominion of Canada many times more than the canals.
May I refer to one suggestion made by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs), which would be worthy of consideration if it would give a real return; he said that perhaps we could impose a charge of one cent a ton. But taking the 1933 traffic through the Welland canal I found that it would yield at one cent a ton about $90,000. So it would not produce enough really to be worth putting on the grain or other traffic that goes through the canals.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext: Say two cents or three cents then.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED IMPOSITION OF TOLLS ON TRAFFIC THROUGH CANADIAN CANALS
speechtext:
Two or three cents would still produce a relatively small amount, not of very much use to Canada in the present economic conditions. Without doubt the commodity that would be chiefly affected by these tolls would be grain, because grain and coal constitute two-thirds of the traffic of the canals; without doubt it would raise costs to the farmer and at the same time give a black eye to the city of Montreal and our other eastern ports by diverting traffic through the other ports that I have already mentioned. Incidentally, may I mention that the grain rate from Fort William to Montreal last year by water averaged about 3-71 cents per bushel while the all-rail rate was 34i cents per hundredweight. My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Turnbull) brought out something to this effect. If all that grain that moved by water to Montreal last season had been carried by rail to Montreal from the head of the lakes at rail rates-which of course would be entirely out of the question-but if it could have been done it would have meant an extra expenditure of about $10,000,000. In regard to the Panama, Suez and Manchester canals it is true, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has said, that they collect tolls. We must realize however that the conditions under which those canals are operated are altogether different from those exisitng in connection with Canadian canals. The Manchester canal is a private commercial enterprise, whereas in Canada our canals are na-

tional. Then, the Suez canal is operated by a privately owned company. True the Panama canal is publicly owned and operated, but we must remember this important point; the difference between the Suez, the Panama and our Canadian canals is that no vessel owner is forced to use either the Suez or the Panama because, if the shipper wishes, he may ignore either of them and take a longer route, thereby arriving at the same point on the globe. However, to do that would require a longer time, and because of that fact, and because through using the Panama or Suez canals he may secure a greater number of cargoes for his ship, he finds that it pays him to take the shorter route offered through using the Panama or Suez canals. Time saving is the important factor, because were it not for these canals it would be necessary to navigate around the southern end of South America or of the African continent. On the other hand, in Canada we have no alternative water route from the western grain fields, unless one wished to use the railways from the head of the lakes. As has already been pointed out, however, the rail rate would be so much higher that it would not be feasible in the marketing of grain. A number of speakers have said that, because of our distance from the seaboard it is important that we should have the lowest possible rates in order that we may compete with countries whose grain fields are closer to the seaboard than are the fields of Canada.
In view of these facts, and in view of statements which have been made by hon. members on both sides of the house I submit to my hon. friend, with the best of intention, that having brought this matter before the House of Commons-and I believe in that he has done very good service, because it is a question which should be discussed in order that it may be threshed out properly-and in view of the very excellent discussion which has taken place, for the time being at any rate he would be doing well to withdraw the resolution and allow further consideration to be given the matter by all classes in the community as well as by hon. members of this house and the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the hon. member concludes the debate I should like to make only a few observations. I make them because of the statements made by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) and in order to remove any misapprehension there may be as to the exact position at the present time with respect to the use of canals and boundary waters. The Boundary Waters treaty of 1909 has a preliminary article reading as follows:
For the purpose of this treaty boundary waters are defined as the waters from main shore to main shore of the lakes and rivers and connecting waterways, or the portions thereof, along which the international boundary between the United States and the Dominion of Canada passes, including all bays, arms and inlets thereof, but not including tributary waters which in their natural channels would flow into such lakes, rivers, and waterways, or waters flowing from such lakes, rivers, and waterways, or the waters of rivers flowing across the boundary.
Article 1 of the 1909 treaty, which is somewhat different from the old treaty of 1871, is as follows:
The high contracting parties agree that the navigation of all navigable boundary waters shall for ever continue free and open for the purposes of commerce to the inhabitants and to the ships, vessels, and boats of both countries equally, subject, however, to any laws and regulations of either country within its own territory, not inconsistent with such privilege of free navigation, and applying equally and without discrimination to the inhabitants, ships, vessels, and boats of both countries.
That, it will be observed, refers to boundary watery, and in article XXVI the treaty of 1871, to which reference was made by the hon. member, refers to other than boundary waters in these words:
The navigation of the river St. Lawrence, ascending and descending from the 45th parallel of north latitude, where it ceases to form the boundary between the two countries, from, to, and into the sea, shall forever remain free and open for the purposes of commerce to the citizens of the United States, subject to any laws and regulations of Great Britain or of the Dominion of Canada, not inconsistent with such privilege of free navigation.
The navigation of the rivers Yukon, Porcupine and Stikine, ascending and descending from, to, and into the sea, shall forever remain free and open for the purposes of commerce to the subjects of Her Britannic Majesty and to the citizens of the United States, subject to any laws and regulations of either country within its own territory, not inconsistent with such privilege of free navigation.
So that in article XXVI of the Treaty of Washington of 1871, which I have just read, we have a declaration with respect to navigation of the St. Lawrence, other than through boundary waters. And in the article I have read with respect to boundary waters you have the same declaration as that contained in the treaty of 1871 with respect to other than boundary waters of the St. Lawrence.
But article 1 of the treaty of 1909 specifically deals with the question of tolls. Perhaps I had better read the article so that there may be no misunderstanding.

He said: I have been a little surprised, Mr. Speaker, to learn that considerable opposition to this resolution would be manifested in this house. We are the only important dominion in the British Empire that has not a flag. South Africa has a flag; India has a flag and New Zealand and Australia each have beautiful flags. On Empire day when my resolution was brought up for the first time, after I had spoken for perhaps thirty-five or forty minutes on the subject, what do you suppose happened? Hon. gentlemen opposite will recall
quite well what happened. As I say, it was on Empire day and I do not think there was a better day in the year to have such a question discussed. Now, there was no intimation until practically six o'clock that the house was to be adjourned, and when the resolution was before the house and everything was set for a first-class debate on this national flag question, along came the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and adjourned the house abruptly at six o'clock, with the result of course that no further debate on the question took place that year. In other words, the question was not allowed to be placed before the people of the country as it should have been. In 1933 when the same resolution was up for discussion, I again spoke on it, taking the stand that if hon. members opposite and the house as a body were not then favourable to the consideration of a distinctive flag for Canada, because of emergency economic conditions, then I was quite willing not to interject at such a time the question of a national flag into the discussion of economic and financial matters, for the reason that it seemed to me important for this house to devote all its time to industrial and commercial subjects, such as the matter of trade, unemployment, and so forth with a view to relieving forthwith the distress of the people. Under these circumstances I took the ground that I would not then urge upon the house a discussion of the question of a distinctive flag for Canada. For that reason and that reason alone I spoke only briefly in 1933; and for that reason I did not place a resolution on the order paper for the session of 1934.
Now it seems to me that we have before us to-day what is very much like a case of trying to steal the other man's thunder, but I say to the hon. member for Nanaimo and to others opposite that that cannot be done by the Conservative party of Canada, nor can it be done by the hon. member for Nanaimo, because the spade work has already been done, and no matter what takes place with respect to the hon. gentleman's resolution at this time he will come second rather than first in the movement for a national flag. But even if he does come second I will lend him my support in order to help the movement along. I want to make it quite plain, once more, not only to the hon. gentleman but to the people of Canada, just where I stand on this question. The people of this country know quite well who put on the order paper of the House of Commons a resolution on behalf of a flag for Canada; they know exactly who first introduced that reso-
Canadian Flag-Mr. McIntosh

lution, and when. They know also that it has already been introduced on more than one occasion.
The hon. member speaks now about opposition. Well, there is no oipposition now of any account. The only opposition to a distinctive flag for Canada comes from the other side of the house-from his own party. There is no opposition on this side, and this question has been kept in the background up to the present time only because of the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite. Everyone in Canada who has read anything on this question knows that. But the opposition at the present time is nothing compared to the opposition that was very apparent a year ago when I had the honour of placing on the order paper a resolution sponsoring a national flag for this country. I had correspondence from every province in Canada, from almost every municipality, town and city, practically from one ocean to the other, and the opposition to a national flag at that time was quite apparent. But I never left one of these letters unanswered; I never let anyone who wrote me opposing a national flag get away with any baseless argument put forward along that line. The result is that to-day after years of hard work, after espousing this cause and doing the cultivating work on behalf of a national flag, after keeping the subject before the people of Canada, in all the provinces, I find that the opposition has now to a very large extent petered out or broken down. I believe that the feeling throughout Canada in the best informed circles is very strongly in favour of a distinctive flag for the dominion.
That being the case, may I direct the attention of the house to the subject matter of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Nanaimo. For instance, he says he stands for a distinctive Canadian flag. That as a matter of fact is an old question now; it lias been before the house for j'ears and I believe there is at the moment a pronounced opinion in favour of it throughout Canada.
Then he goes on to say that it must be a national flag. How could it be anything else. He also says that the union jack must be in it. If he has the idea that his riding can by any stretch of the imagination be classified as the most British in Canada on account of the fact that a great number of the people there were born overseas, in England, Scotland, Ireland or Wales, then he has another guess coming, because I repudiate any such statement. If any person born in Canada, born in Quebec or any other province, is loyal to his king, his flag, his country, he is just as good a Britisher as anyone else. I make no apology for a statement of that kind; I do not care what his creed or his national extraction may be; he can be just as British as those who are born overseas or those directly descended from citizens bom in the British Isles. That is self evident.
Another point advanced by the hon. member is that we should have on the fly of the flag a maple leaf. I do not think I ever made an address on the flag question in any part of Canada that I did not say I thought the maple leaf would make a very suitable design, but I did not think I had any right to come before parliament and say what the design on a Canadian flag should be. I thought then and I think so now a special committee of the house should be convened, consider the question thoroughly and adopt a resolution thereon. It might take a year or two to decide upon the design for a Dominion flag. If a special committee were convened and evidence adduced from well defined parts of Canada by having representatives of many of our national organizations appear before the committee and if parliament were to offer a prize of $1,000 or so for the best design, we would get not only one but hundreds and thousands of artistic designs, just as in Australia, and from these designs guided by the good sense of the committee and the House of Commons, we could certainly pick a flag that would best symbolize Canada among the nations of the world. The job is no small one; it is big; it cannot be done in a day or a week or a month, and it is something to which any party attempting to deal with it should give its very best attention. Therefore, one of the

strongest committees that can be got together in the house ought to be appointed and it should go into the flag question thoroughly and report to the house. Then the government of the day could very properly act on that report.

I believe the war veterans of Canada passed a resolution practically favouring a distinctive flag for the dominion; at least they went so far as to put themselves on record that they were not opposed to it. In my address to the house on Empire day, Monday, May 25, 1931, I incorporated their resolution, because I thought it was very important to put the War Veterans of Canada on record with regard to a national flag. Hon. members who wish to turn up my address can -read for themselves what the members of the Canadian Legion thought then of the question now before the house.
Further than that, members of the Canadian Weekly Newspaper Association, a national organization, went on record at London in 1929, favouring a distinctive flag. Since then literally hundreds and thousands of resolutions have been passed by organizations, clubs and gatherings of one nature or another in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag. The Kiwanians in convention assembled at Windsor, September 15, 1931, where representative business men from the Atlantic coast attended, went on record in favour of a distinctive national flag. From that day to this the sentiment in favour of a national flag has been growing-gathering splendid momentum.

Such a view of it, if held, springs to my mind from a dangerous illusion; the illusion, only too common to-day, that those two words ''old" and "out of date" necessarily mean the same thing. That the idea of a flag is an old one is unquestionably true; it is so old that it makes its appearance in the very dawn of civilization. The human race, ever since it began to march at all, has never been able to march without the guidance of some symbol; and the function of such symbols has been two fold-they point out to mankind a better way for the future and they remind them of good that lias been achieved in the past.

But for our part we have never seen any reason why Canada should not have sueb a flag; and there are many reasons why, when inter-empire gatherings such as that at Ottawa are held, there should be some method of distinguishing the Canadian colours.

Candidly, we do not see -why Canada should not have a flag that is at once British as well as Canadian. The governments of the dominions have adopted national flags. Why there should be any fuss about Canada having a flag that would be pronounced Canadian as well as British we cannot understand. This opposition to a "Canadian Flag" is silly sentiment and should not stand in the way of our government adopting a Canadian flag.
The Brockville Recorder and Times says:
If opponents of a Canadian national flag, in which the union jack could be embodied, were consistent, they would instantly demand that Canada abandon its red ensign and return to the flag of the British merchant marine. There is, however, no demand for such abandonment. Why should there not be equal approval of the institution of a Canadian national flag to fly on land? Mr. Chamberlain probably wonders. So do a great many others, who are quite unable to fathom the reasoning of those who object to such a proceeding.
The Perth Courier, a leading weekly, says:
There is no thought either in any Liberal's or Conservative's brain to do away with the time-honoured union jack in our national flag. We all love the old flag and its Christian three-cross design too well to abandon it for any other. No other flag has so wonderful a history or has earned so loving a tribute from its far-flung peoples as this emblem of the empire; and so we in Canada must honour this feeling and all the sentiments involved by retaining in the most prominent corner of any flag that may be adopted this old union jack with its historical and fond memories.
The Hamilton Herald makes this statement:
If prejudice could he put aside and reason were allowed to rule, it would be easy to make a compromise arrangement satisfactory to all parties.
The Brantford Expositor thinks that if an agreement eould be reached whereby a Canadian device would appear on the union jack it would promote an intenser feeling of patriotism and citizenship not only for the dominion but for the empire. Canadians, it says, are surely not afraid of an emblem that would characterize the flag as their own.
The Kingston Whig-Standard, in concluding an editorial, makes this statement:
There is no reason why Canada should not have its own distinctive flag. It will make us no less loyal and no less a part of the British Empire. Now that the idea of a distinctive Canadian flag has been publicly adopted by the Kiwanians of Ontario, Quebec and the maritime districts, it is quite possible that the matter will receive wider attention than it has received heretofore, and that something tangible will result therefrom.
fMr. McIntosh.]
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I believe it would be only right for the house to have a clear-cut and complete debate on this question, and not merely a clear-cut debate but a recorded vote, so that we will know exactly where every member representing a Canadian constituency stands on this question of a distinctively Canadian flag. My opinion is that if that were done the house would carry this resolution, and if it did, the next step would be to set up a parliamentary committee which would investigate this question from every angle, and have the report endorsed by parliament and thereafter at the opportune time have it decided what flag design should be adapted. The success of the whole undertaking would depend upon the committee established as well as upon the direction of parliament. Of course, time would be required to settle all the details. I believe that not only the house if allowed a free hand but Canada as a nation and our empire's king are all in favour of every dominion having a distinctive flag of its own, and any opposition trumped up in this house or out of it is merely shortsighted opposition. So far as I am concerned as an hon. member of this house I would like to see parliamentary action taken on this resolution immediately so that in the very near future we can have the flag problem worked out in such a way that Canada will have a truly national flag that will take its place proudly among the most beautiful, the most honoured and the most beloved of the many national symbols floating on high the earth around.

Since this depression commenced we have had a resolution to change our system of finance, to inflate, deflate and reflate our money, and resolutions covering other subjects. As the hon. member has said, he was the first to introduce this matter.
We are still in the depression and another resolution to change our flag is brought forward. Is there anything that is inviolable? Is there anything that is safe? Is there anything in which we can put our faith? Is there anything that is not going to change? I recall the twenty-eighth verse of the twenty-second chapter of Proverbs, which reads: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set. Of all the ancient landmarks in the world to-day, in my humble opinion the union jack is the most sacred. I remember being up in the county of Grey where I go quite frequently and visiting the son of a pioneer who had settled on a farm in 1850. He was repairing a line fence and his man was going along the fence and taking down some rotten rails. He came across an old, roughly hewn stake which had some roughly carved marks upon it. Like so many

Canadian Flag-Mr. MacNicol
young men-I do not mean this to apply to all young men as I am a great admirer of the youth of this generation-he was about to destroy that stake when the son of the pioneer stopped him and said:	Hands off,
that is the stake placed by my father and the surveyor in 1850; I want it to remain there.
In the union jack we have three very ancient landmarks, all going back into mythology. They go farther back than any other landmark of which I know. We have the landmark of the cross of St. Patrick. That was the cross carried by St. Patrick into the Emerald Isle where he taught the words of the Nazarene. Then we have the cross of St. Andrew. Mythology tells us that St. Andrew was martyred in Greece and his body transported miraculously to bonnie Scotland. Then we have the cross of St. George. Mythology tells us that this was the cross which was on the white banner of St. George when he appeared before the English armies and saved them from the Saracens. These are ancient landmarks and I say to those who would support this resolution: Remember the landmarks that our fathers have set and remove them not.
It has been stated that other dominions have a distinctive flag. That is true, but Canada is the greatest of all dominions, and are we to be leaders or merely followers? Simply because another dominion has a distinctive flag is not a conclusive reason Why Canada should adopt one. I read very carefully the debate which took place in the South African house on this question, and if I do not miss my guess, there will be millions in South Africa, Australia and New Zealand who will be very happy if this house does not follow in their footsteps. I hope this house rejects this resolution and decides not to pull down the union jack and erect some other flag in its place. The union jack has tradition behind it; it is the official flag of this country and it should not be pulled down. I hope this resolution will be rejected by a large majority.

educated and gifted orator like my hon. friend across the aisle and like my good friend on this side was able to present an argument which for sheer lack of defenders of the union jack was agreed to and the union jack was pulled down. I hope defenders will not be lacking in this house. If they are, I shall be very much surprised.
A few moments ago I said that perhaps some good comes out of an educational debate even in times like this, and I believe that some good may come out of this one. The mover of the resolution has suggested the maple leaf in place of the arms of Canada. Well, if he had proposed a resolution to put the maple leaf on the fly of the flag which is flown over the legations, or on the ships of the Canadian merchant or government marine, I should have no particular objection, because in each of those spheres there is competition, and if the people of Canada desire to have one emblem or another, that is their business. But on land, on the north half of this continent, there is no competition. I have a recollection of coming here on the first day of the imperial conference, and as I walked up past the post office, where all the flags of the dominions were flying outside the walls, I saw various stripes and bars and colours. But when I passed by that building and came up the main walk in front of this building and saw the flag that was flying at the mast of	the memorial tower, I was
never so proud of any flag as I was then of the union jack. It was to me the finest of flags and its colours stood out more beautifully than any I had ever seen except the colours on the battleship Hood, in Victoria harbour a few years ago, where I had gone with a committee to receive the admiral. The colours of our flag, displayed on that opening day of the imperial conference, were more brilliant than any other such colours I had seen before-the blue, the red and the white. The blue recalled to my mind the crest of the waves as one crosses the ocean, a beautiful blue. The red suggested the sacrifice of the British people down through the ages, marking the pathways for the ships of commerce, leading to every harbour throughout the world-not for military glory alone but for the glories of peace as well. And the white stood for the honour of our nation, standing like a beacon light before the world.
The union jack, with its three colours, its three crosses, is complete. You cannot add anything to it. If you attempt to add to it you add not, and if you take away from it you take from its completeness. There might

Canadian Flag-Mr. White (Mount Royal)
be some reason for enacting legislation, if there is not at present such legislation, to make necessary the flying of one flag on land in this country. I have in mind what the late Mr. Justice Logie said when he opened court at Welland on October 20, 1931. When he arrived he observed flying on the flagstaff of the courthouse a flag other than the union jack. He knew that the official flag in Canada is the union jack, and that this flag should be on 'the flagstaff of all government buildings, and he made the following remarks to the grand jury, at that time, as reported by the Mail and Empire:
Gentlemen,-when I arrived for this session I observed a monstrosity at the head of the court flagstaff, a cross between an admiralty flag and a patchwork quilt. I have ordered the sheriff to take that thing down. It is important and proper that the union jack be flown here, especially as there are so many foreigners in this district. That thing at the head of the mast now is not the flag to be flown oveT His Majesty's courthouse. I hope you will bring in a recommendation that a new flag be purchased. In the meantime, the proper union jack will be flown, even if it is in tatters.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that our highways are to-day cluttered up with all sorts of monstrosities in the way of flags, and the time ha3 come when there should be a rebirth of patriotic spirit in this country, such as there is across the line, where they fly only the stars and stripes. I give that nation to the south of us credit for teaching their people to be loyal to their flag and to fly it and it alone on all public occasions, and I say that we should not have the highways of Canada cluttered up with a regiment of monstrosities. If, therefore, the resolution before the house to-night does nothing more than to direct the attention of the Canadian people to the fact that the time has come for a proper realization once more that on land the union jack is the official flag of this country, then the resolution serves a good purpose. The people might learn further that when that flag is flown it must be attached to the mast with the wide part of the cross of St. Andrew along the top. Quite often we see it upside down, and perhaps Judge Logie witnessed something of the sort. The flag should be flown properly, and on land the official flag is the union jack. I do not see -why this is not taught in the schools; I contend that this should be done, so that we might not have all this discussion about changing flags and getting a new flag. All such discussion should be a thing of the past, and the boys and girls of this country should be taught the full meaning of the flag with the triple cross which flies over land inhabited by a quarter of the world's population.
I yield to no one in my love for Canada. I am a Canadian of the fourth generation, the first generation of which was a Scottish veteran of a Scottish regiment that took part in Quatre Bras and Waterloo. I glory in the achievements of Canadians, and I respect and admire the achievements of all creeds and races and colours; I have nothing to say against any race, because I realize that we are all God's creatures and should do our best. Canadians have every reason to be proud of what this country has accomplished, and when I hear this talk about pulling down the flag I think of the regiments that left the shores of Canada between the years 1914 and 1918. Many of the men that went overseas failed to come back, but the flags came back and today right across Canada you will see those flags hanging in our churches and in our great cathedrals and public halls. Those flags Should remain there, a perpetual memorial to those who did not come back; and to those Who are willing to see them pulled down, I say that if the union jack is to fly over the peace tower where the names of our fallen heroes are to be inscribed until they say "pull it down," it will fly until the crack of doom.
