He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting this resolution to the house hon. members will note that I have followed the form of my resolution presented on February 6, of last year, upon which occasion I was supported by some of my friends. Later the resolution went to the bottom of the order paper and was not reached again during the session.
At the time I introduced my resolution of a year ago I drew attention to a number of anomalies in prices, particularly those anomalies in the prices of farm products in the raw state, and the prices of the same products after processing. Upon that occasion I desired, as indicated in my resolution, to have the research council during the recess period go into the matter of these anomalies in prices, in order that legislation could have been presented at this session based on their report. This evening it is not my intention to deal, as I did last year, with particular items, but rather to speak in general terms. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) introduced his motion of February 2, dealing with some of the matters contained in my resolution my inclination was to withdraw from the order paper the resolution standing in my name, in the hope that the committee to be set up would deal effectively with the questions I had in mind. Since then, however, I have given considerable thought to the matter and have come to the conclusion that the committee which has been set up, sitting as it will be for only a few hours a day, a few days each week, cannot by any means meet the situation I have in mind. Its efforts

Production and Distribution
will be entirely inadequate to deal with the great volume of business which will come before it, and for that reason I believe the work of that committee might well be supplemented by the investigation I propose.
After the committee was set up about a week ago I noticed headlines in the newspapers referring to it as a committee on mass buying, and those newspaper articles prompted me to proceed with my resolution. The question of mass buying does not in any sense enter into the resolution standing in my name. The people with whom I am* concerned do not consider mass buying an evil. As I view it, mass buying is only a system which has grown up during the last few years which has for its purpose the overcoming of an evil, and cannot be considered an evil in itself from the consumer's viewpoint. Further, I have proceeded with the resolution because I believe the method adopted by the government, namely that of appointing a special committee, is altogether too cumbersome, and it will take too long to accomplish anything. On account of the urgency of this matter I believe the suggestion I have offered should be accepted, so as to supplement the work of the committee, in the hope that some remedial legislation may be effected while the depression exists. If we go through this depression without doing something along the lines I have indicated I am afraid that, in the event of another depression in a few years conditions would be found to be worse than those now prevailing. Particularly would this apply to those who are suffering most in these days, namely the poor people.
There is another reason why I desire to present this resolution, and that is in relation to the personnel of the committee that has been appointed. I am going to ask the Prime Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, if he thinks it is just and right that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) should be permitted to sit in judgment on that committee. I am going to read a letter written by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to a gentleman by the name of Hermiston, and which was published in a paper called the Parliamentary Critic, Ottawa. The letter, dated Ottawa, January 19, is as follows:
Dear Mr. Hermiston,

I have your letter of the 17th and thank you very much for the illustrations attached to show the evil influence of the department and chain store system.
We are now continuing the investigation and hope to build up a pretty strong case. The information you have given will be useful.
Yours very truly,
H. H. Stevens.
In view of that letter I say in all seriousness that as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has prejudged the question he ought not be allowed to sit in judgment on a committee of that kind, and I am bringing it to the attention of the government in the hope that they will take my objection into their very serious consideration.
Last year when I presented this resolution I dealt largely with the question of wool and woollen clothing, for the reason that woollen clothing is so necessary in the part of the country from which I come, and also because there are so many people, even those who are raising wool, who are not able to buy it back in its manufactured form, and are therefore suffering from the want of it. I believe that the resolution I am presenting strikes at the very root of this depression, and that if the matter complained of were remedied it would go a long way towards our recovery from this depression. Certainly when another depression comes along, as they appear to do periodically, it will bear much more heavily upon the people if action along this line is not taken in the meantime.
The outstanding feature of the present depression so far as the farming community is concerned has been the unprecedented decline in the prices of commodities, more particularly farm products, without a corresponding fall in the prices of manufactured goods. Our trouble is due not only to the fact that farm prices have depreciated enormously, but also to the disparity between the decrease in farm prices and the decline in the prices of manufactured products. While manufactured products are lower in price, as we will all admit, they have not dropped to the low levels reached by the prices of raw materials and natural products generally. I repeat, as I have stated before in this house as well as elsewhere, that a depressed agriculture, such as we have in Canada to-day, is one of the main reasons why we have falling revenues, unemployment, the railway problem and a good many of our other major problems. Let me give a few figures which will prove what I have said, that the prices of farm products have fallen to a greater extent than the prices of manufactured products.

For succeeding years, still on the basis of 1926 prices, the values of farm products required to buy one dollars' worth of manufactured goods were: in 1928, ninety-four cents' worth; in 1920, ninety-two cents' worth; in 1930, $1.09 worth; in 1931, $1.33 worth; in 1932, $1.44 worth, and in 1933, $1.49 worth. By this it may be seen that the manufacturing industries did not suffer to anything like the same extent as the farming industry. I contend, and these figures go to prove, that if farm products were on the same basis as other products, if one dollar's worth of farm products would buy one dollar's worth of manufactured products, we would still be able to buy and sell, and the country would not be in the condition it is in to-day. But when we have to give almost $1.50 worth of farm products to buy one dollar's worth of manufactured goods, recovery is almost impossible so far as the farming industry is concerned.
On the second day of this month the Prime Minister introduced a resolution appointing a committee to inquire into some of the matters which are mentioned in my resolution. At that time, speaking to that resolution, I stated that I believed that combines, the high tariffs and special duties and other regulations of the National Revenue department were largely responsible for the wide spread in prices between natural products and the same products in a manufactured state. The question has often been asked why it is that this depression appears to bear so much more heavily upon the farmers and the labouring 
classes than former depressions did, and particular reference is made when the question is asked to the depression of 1020-1922. The answer that I have given, and I believe it is the best answer available, is that tariffs are higher in Canada to-day than they have ever been before in the history of this country, and the manufacturers in Canada, in spite of what may be said, are taking advantage of those high tariffs. The labouring men and fhe farmers cannot obtain by any stretch of the imagination any benefit from these high tariffs. This is largely the reason why the depression is bearing so much more heavily to-day upon the farming community than it did previously. The very fact that the manufacturers are taking advantage of the high tariff compels the farmers and labouring people to pay higher prices for the products they need than otherwise would be the case. This has been denied many times from the other side of the house; hon. members opposite try to make out that the tariff is not responsible for increases in prices, but I remember last year when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) brought down his budget he stated that many manufacturing industries were operating in the red because they were able to operate only twenty-five, fifty or sixty per cent of their capacity. He stated that that was why they required higher tariff protection. To my mind that is an admission that these manufacturing industries are taking advantage of the tariff. If they are not, and this is something I should like investigated, it is because there are too many industries in certain lines attempting to operate in Canada.
Business in all lines is calling out for some relief. The resolution of the Prime Minister and the setting up of a committee has met with a good deal of favour, but so did the resolution which I presented a year ago. I contend that had that resolution been adopted last year we could have been in a fair way to having some legislation to remedy the conditions of which I complained. Even now it is not too late. I cannot see how this committee, which will sit only a few hours a day for a few days each week, can do any more than touch the fringe of this big question. The president of the United States has been given wide powers to deal with just such matters as were mentioned in my resolution, and he is making a determined effort to deal with the problem. He is dealing with it in a big way, and I believe that if there has been an improvement in conditions in Canada it is because of what is being done in the United States. I believe that that country is an indispensable factor in the world recovery

Production and Distribution
which we all hope will come very soon. It will be noticed that the United States is beginning to deal with reality and is now tackling the tariff problem with a view to reducing duties and bringing about greater trade with other nations of the world. That country realizes, as must every country sooner or later, that economic exclusiveness, as it has been termed here, tends to make the problem harder to solve.
I have always been at a loss to know why our representatives at the conference held at Ottawa in 1932 did not endeavour to have some provision made whereby the better quality clothing manufactured in Great Britain, which could be sold here at a price lower than the poorer quality manufactured in Canada, could continue to be brought into the country Such a measure would have increased the market in Great Britain for some of our products. I know the answer is that the government wanted to give employment to people engaged in the textile industry, but I know that people in my part of the country are not buying simply because they have no purchasing power. Quite often I hear men say that they have not had a suit of clothes for the last five years. If the retail stores throughout the country were doing the business they would be doing if conditions were right, many of the men in the textile industry who might be laid off could be engaged in selling goods over the counter and be just as profitably employed.
Surely the time has come when we should do something more than just appoint a committee to investigate a few things. As I said, this committee will be sitting a few hours a day in an attempt to deal with this great problem. There is a need of some drastic measure when the people who produce raw materials are not able to buy them back after they are processed. I hope this government will soon realize that there are other people who should be considered besides the manufacturers. In tackling this problem we are tackling a problem too large to be handled in the way that this government is attempting to handle it. During the last two years when I have had this resolution in mind and when it has appeared upon the order paper I have received many letters from all across Canada. I think the people of Canada would be solidly behind the government if they would take hold of this problem in a big way but from what I have seen in some of the papers I am afraid that to a certain extent the people are of the same opinion as myself, namely, that the government is not going after it in a big enough way. I should like to quote part of a long editorial which appeared in the Times-
Herald of Moose Jaw. This editorial deals with this very matter, and the concluding words are these:
The problem that was shelved a year ago has suddenly become urgent for political reasons, and in order to forestall a demand on the part of the opposition for a far-reaching inquiry under the Research Council Act, the government prefers the longer and roundabout way of a parliamentary inquiry, which it can always hold well in hand, and which a "steering committee " of the protected manufacturers can guide along the lines desired.
I am not prepared to go quite as far as that editorial. I hope the government is in earnest, but there are others besides the Moose Jaw Times-Herald who do not believe that the government is in earnest in trying to solve this problem. This is the conclusion I have reached from the many letters I have received. One man said to me that this was a Liberal policy and he wondered how the government could go ahead with anything like that. He then quoted the words of the Prime Minister who said on one occasion: Converts always can be depended upon to make a failure of anything they undertake to do. My final word is this: Let us adopt the best method possible; if it is the intention of the government that this committee should deal with the mass buying problem, all well and good, but let us have some earnest endeavour to do something in connection with these price spreads.

speechtext:
I really had not thought of saying anything in regard to this resolution, but while the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) was speaking a few thoughts came to my mind. I would point out to the house, as we have had occasion to point out many times before, that in the question of spread in prices as between the producer and the consumer there is no one who suffers more than the farmer, and I would discuss this question from the standpoint of the farmers, since I am a representative of farmers. No one suffers more than the farmer, for this reason, that he gets it both ways, whether it is on what he produces or on what he buys. If it is a question of wheat, then the price we receive for our wheat is based upon the world price, and that takes into account all costs that have to be paid between the time the commodity leaves the farmer's wagon and the time it gets to the consumer. The farmer pays all the freight,
Production and Distribution

all the commission charges, everything that has to be paid between the time it leaves his waggon and the time it reaches the consumer. And similarly with the things he buys; the price he has to pay for what he buys is the price the manufacturer gets plus the price that the distributors, however many they may be, have to be paid for their services, and the freight rates. The farmer has to pay for all that, and therefore the farmer more than any other class suffers by this spread in prices. To put it another way, the farmer sells everything at wholesale prices and buys back everything at retail prices.
A committee has now been set up to study the question of mass buying by the department and the chain stores, and so on, but here is something which that committee will be faced with when it comes to investigate this matter. If the committee tries to regulate this spread between what the producer gets and what the consumer pays it will find that it has a conflict on its hands, because the mass buying on the part of the department and chain stores is an attempt to lower this difference between what the producer gets and what the consumer pays. I do not see therefore how the committee will solve the problem with these two conflicting interests to be considered; at any rate it cannot solve both at the same time.
The ordinary consumer in the city suffers of course, but he does not suffer the double burden that the farmer has to bear. The consumer has to pay all the cost, and I think we may as well turn our attention to the fact that so much of this cost is taken up in distribution. There is the problem that confronts us. We have solved the question of production; we have not solved the question of economical distribution. I remember that at one of our United Farmer's meetings a good many years ago an old farmer from a small town in northern Manitoba gave this illustration. He said that in his town of Fox-warren there were one day four commercial travellers, one selling soap, another candies, another tobacco and, I think, the fourth one was selling matches-it does not matter what it was; maybe it was Eddy matches.

I imagine that between the price which the hon. member for Lincoln gets for such a fork and what I had to pay there is a wide spread. What the spread is I do not know, but I hope that the committee, of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) is to be chairman, will investigate that situation and see whether he will solve that problem by attacking mass buying in the department and chain stores, because these methods have been introduced to help to solve the problem of the spread between the price that the producer receives and the price the consumer pays. I think he will have to do a little bit of running with the hare and hunting with the hounds when he deals with this matter.
Undoubtedly there is a problem that confronts us, and I emphasize again the fact that the farmer gets it both ways, both on what he produces and on what he buys. I happen to know that a certain man sold twenty ducks, dressed-and ducks are not the easiest thing in the world to dress and clean-and the return to this producer was less than 20 cents apiece; the whole net return was $3.95. I presume the people in the city who consumed those ducks paid 10 or 12 cents a pound at least, and perhaps a good deal more. Illustrations might be multiplied indefinitely to show the very wide spread that exists. I think it was brought out in the milk inquiry that was held in Winnipeg that the man who drove the milk wagon distributing the milk received more than twice as much for his work as the farmer who produced the milk. While this question

If that can be done and if any person is able to show ns just how it can be done, I shall be only too glad to listen to him.

I should like to say just a 'word or two, addressing my remarks more directly to the resolution before us than to the affairs of the [DOT]committee that has been set up by the house. I feel myself precluded from discussing that if I desire to obey the rules, which I think are clear that we are not permitted to discuss in this chamber the activities of a committee.
The resolution that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) proposes is that under the provisions of the Research Council Act, or by other means, an inquiry should be made into the causes underlying the wide spread between the prices of raw products and the prices of goods manufactured from such products. May I suggest to the mover of the resolution-and to this degree I shall have to transgress what I know to be the Tules-that the first action of the committee set up was to invite the bureau of statistics and the president of the national research council, together with the official in charge of the Combines Act, to make an immediate study of all the material, documents, data and so forth at present in the hands of government departments and to correlate all this information in preparation for treatment by the committee. In other words, the very thing he is now asking is actually under way at the present moment. As I say, it is quite contrary to the rules for me or any other hon. member to enter into a discussion, first, of the activities of a committee, and, second, of a debate that has already been closed by the action of this house, namely in passing a resolution and appointing a committee based upon it. Therefore I am precluded by the rules from carrying that further. I have, as I say, transgressed them to the extent of conveying that information to the hon. member.
I might perhaps invite the house for a moment to consider the Research Council Act. To speak now of that act which is specifically referred to in the resolution before us, the question is whether under that act this matter is properly 'covered. I merely mention that; I think the act has more to
do with scientific and industrial research and standardization. One of the reasons why the research council was invited to join with the bureau of statistics in a study of this matter was the scientific knowledge possessed by the expert officials of the council and particularly the possible assistance that might be secured by furtheT standardization. But I might say to the hon. member that in the bureau of statistics there are some highly skilled and competent officials, economists we would be well justified in terming them, who can give and are now giving close study to the very matters to which he refers. In the light of what I have said to the hon. member, I do not see that there would be anything gained by pressing this motion to a vote.
I am sure both my hon. friends who have spoken will excuse me if I do not follow them in a discussion of the matters to which they have referred, because, as I say, they are all matt-eTs which I think are more or less out of order under this particular resolution, having been dealt with in connection with the committee that has been set up. But I would be unfair to myself and other hon. gentlemen on this side of the house if I were not to say that we fully appreciate, just as keenly as do hon. members opposite, the tremendous importance of the welfare^ of 'the agriculturists of this country. Speaking for myself, I am profoundly impressed with that. I know full well what the prosperity of the agriculturists means to Canada and am just as keenly anxious as it is possible to be to do everything we can to find a solution for the problems with which they are confronted.
I should like, however, to say to my hon. friends that perhaps more progress may be made in the interests of the agriculturists and other producers of primary products if we could approach the question with some degree of unanimity of purpose. I assure them that I have no desire to make the fate of the agriculturists a question of political view, and if they will, I certainly will approach the question with one desire and that is to do the best we can to find a solution for these problems. I do not think there is any need for me to say more at the moment. In the light of the facts that I have indicated, I would suggest to the hon. member that the resolution might be allowed to drop or to be withdrawn.

That, in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government of Canada reopen negotiations with the government of the United States of America with a view of bringing about a satisfactory reciprocal trade agreement between Canada and the United States, whereby the natural products of Canada, that is, the products of the sea, the farm, the mines and the forests, and including fish, lumber, wheat, cattle, etc., should have free entry into the United States in exchange for the admission of certain goods from the United States of America, which in the interests of both countries may be admitted into Canada, free from customs tariffs.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in rising to support
this resolution I would say that it is worded in exactly the same terms as one which I moved in this house last year. I think it will be agreed that on that occasion there was a fair and perhaps full discussion of this very important matter. At that time certain objections were made because I introduced the resolution in the manner in which I did and at the time I did. If I remember correctly objection was also made to the fact that I used the word "expedient," that in the opinion of this house it is expedient that the government of Canada reopen negotiations with the government of the United States. After the discussion I looked it up in the dictionary and found that after all is said and done the word "expedient" "is not such a harsh or unsuitable one; it means "desirable." So I could just as well have used the word "desirable"; it would have meant the same thing.
Further in regard to the wording of the resolution, may I say that as long as the government and this house will accept the resolution I am willing to amend it as far as possible so as to meet the wishes of the government and the house; I am not committed to any particular form of resolution regarding this very important matter. I do say, however, as to my reason for reintroducing it at this session, that I am sincere in the

Trade with United States-Mr. Duff
matter. I am not introducing it in any partisan spirit, but I feel, as I have felt for a great many years and did feel long before the reciprocity agreement was introduced in this house in the session of 1911, that it is in the interests of this country and the United States as well that these two countries, situated side by side, should do a greater volume of trade one with another on a reciprocal basis. Therefore I say that if it is necessary that the motion be amended in some slight degree I have no particular objection to that being done.
I said a moment ago that there were other objections raised last year. One was that when I introduced the motion it was premature. That might be, because at that time, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) pointed out, the government of the United States had only recently been changed, and the president-elect had not yet taken charge of the affairs of the government. Another reason given by the Prime Minister was that there was to be a world economic conference held in London, at which among other things the subject of tariffs was to be discussed. In his speech on that occasion the Prime Minister said:
But there is another reason, and I put it to the house as being, I submit, a conclusive reason why at this time, after this discussion, which cannot be helpful, we should not adopt any resolution that would involve the possibility of being taken as an indication of a division of opinion. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the other day directed attention to the fact that a draft annotated agenda for the monetary and economic conference had been issued. I indicated that while that is a draft agenda only, it is now published, and any person who so desired might * avail himself of the opportunity to read it. Among the items on that agenda for consideration you will perhaps recall that after some difficulty this was added:
5. Tariff and treaty policy.
A. Tariff policy:
(1)	Cessation of tariff increases.
(2)	Reduction of tariffs.
(3)	Special aspects of the tariff problem.
(4)	Method of procedure.
Now, sir, since the Prime Minister knew at that time what the agenda of the worid economic conference was to be, I can understand his reason for asking me then that my resolution should stand. As will be remembered, I had no opportunity either to withdraw it or to ask that a vote be taken on it. However, that conference met, and although the United States was represented there no action was taken in regard to tariffs. I think in view of that fact, and view of the serious situation in certain parts of this country, that I am justified to-night in raising my voice in
this house in order to try again to impress on this parliament and the government the necessity of arranging some reciprocal treaty with our great neighbour to the south.
I was pleased to-night when the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mir. White), speaking in regard to the flag, referred to a meeting in Saint John, New Brunswick, some fifty or sixty years ago at which meeting there were present James G. Blaine, a candidate for the presidency of the United States, and Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, who was then Prime Minister of Canada. The hon. member for Mount Royal told us that at that meeting, in their speeches, referring to the flag, they both said there was no reason why the two flags should not fly side by side. If the United States flag and the union jack can fly side by side, is there any reason why this great country and the great country to the south should not be able to trade with each another more freely than they do? Look at the map of the northern part of this continent; if it were not for the fact that the two parts are in different colours most of us would not know where the United Stated ends on the north and where Canada begins; we would not know that Canada's territory ends at the forty-ninth parallel and that the United States begins there. Since Canada is divided from the United States only by the forty-ninth parallel, an imaginary lime, and the great lakes, is there any reason why New Brunswick should not trade with the state of Maine just as freely as New Brunswick trades with Nova Scotia? Is there any reason why New York state should not trade with the province of Quebec as easily as Quebec trades with Ontario? We might say the same of adjoining points along the border until we reach the Pacific coast and come to Point Roberts and the Fraser river dividing Canada from the United States. God and nature never intended that the United States and Canada should not have a fair and equitable arrangement whereby one could trade with the other.
There is no doubt in my mind that because of tariffs and restrictions existing between Canada and the United States, conditions in Canada are not as good as they might be. Since for the last fifty or sixty years we have had oeirtadn policies in Canada I can understand that it would be difficult immediately to do away entirely with those restrictions and barriers, yet I am fully convinced that the adoption of better trade relations between these two contiguous countries would be in the best interests of Canada and the Canadian people and the people of the United States.
736	COMMONS
Trade with United States-Mr. Duff
Although the rules will not; permit me to quote, may I say that in this chamber a speech was made only a few days ago in which this question was discussed. Answering some speeches which have been made by hon. members on this side of the house the Prime Minister stated that he would not sign a lopsided pact of reciprocity. May I say to him I am with him heart and soul in that statement. I do not want to see nor is there any need of any lopsided treaty. To my mind there is no reason why the peoples of the United States and Canada cannot get together and make a treaty or agreement which would be satisfactory to both countries. The argument was used that the reciprocal trade arrangement suggested in 1911 was not a treaty, but was only an agreement. I believe it was the Prime Minister who said that he would not agree to an agreement and that if anything was done it would have to be in the shape of a treaty. It is immaterial to me whether it is an agreement or a treaty because I am convinced that if an arrangement was made if only for a few months it would benefit a great many people in the Dominion of Canada.
Speaking on that point, let me say that I should like to give credit to this government for what it has done in connection with an arrangement for which I have argued, talked and fought for the last twenty years. I refer to the modus vivendi arrangement with the United States. For years I have tried to get that into effect. I urged the late government, the present one and the department to let United States vessels come into this country and do business so that they might buy bait and ice supplies, and land their fish in bond and send it to the United States. Last year, quite properly, this government decided that they would allow the United States vessels to do those very things I have mentioned. The government agreed to make that arrangement for a period of six months. If it was good business to make a modus vivendi arrangement for six months why would it not be just as good to have a reciprocity treaty for six months, a year, two years or as long as both contracting parties could agree?
My only objection to the modus vivendi is that in my opinion, so far as the maritime provinces are concerned-and they are most affected-from a business standpoint there is no reason why the government could not send word to-morrow to the government of the United States saying, "Come in as often as you like, stay as long as you like, and do as much business as you like with us." There is no reason why the government of Canada

should not say to the government of the United States, "We will let you bring your fish into Nova Scotia ports; we will let you land those fish and buy ice and boxes from those who make ice and boxes, and we will let you hire labourers to pack the fish and use our trains to carry them to their destination." Surely there could be no objection to that. And if it is good business to do that for six months, there is no reason why we should quibble as to whether or not a reciprocal trade arrangement is an agreement or a treaty.
I notice in the speech from the throne the following expression:
The temporary trade arrangements made with Germany and Austria have been further extended. Canadian products are now receiving most favoured tariff treatment in those countries in exchange for the grant of our intermediate tariff on their products.
Then if hon. members will turn to the estimates they will find that a vote of $200,000 is asked from this parliament to expand trade in European countries. Surely if it is good business to make an arrangement with Austria and Germany, if it is good business to vote $200,000 to extend our trade with those countries, is it not even more in the interests of the Canadian people to arrange to spend money, if necessary-and I do not think it would be necessary-to make an arrangement with the United States so that we may do business with the people on the other side of the boundary line?
If we could make an arrangement with the United States I can see no reason why our cattle should have to be shipped from Alberta to Quebec or Montreal and from those points overseas to the English market when, within three or four hundred miles of this country, ' we have a market. I cannot understand why other Canadian products should have to be sent long distances when we should be able to buy and sell in the United States market.
In discussing a resolution introduced to-day by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon), the statement was made that the United States had taken retaliatory action because of a certain agreement or treaty which was made a couple of years ago within the British Empire. I said two years ago, when the Ottawa conference was being discussed in this House of Commons and an arrangement had been made whereby if certain goods from the western prairies did not go entirely through Canadian channels they would have to pay a duty of six cents per bushel, that I was very much afraid the United States might adopt a similar measure under which they would retaliate against us for taking that action. I noticed the other

Trade with United States-Mr. Duff
day there was an effort in the United States to have the president put a ten per cent duty on all goods going through Canadian channels destined to the United States.
Mr, BENNETT:	May I correct the hon.
gentleman? That referred to the item which was passed in the first budget of Mr. Robb by which a ten per cent further preference was given if the imports came through Canadian ports, and the United States had some years ago introduced a measure to meet that situation. It was introduced again by a senator from Maine and had nothing at all to do with the Ottawa conference.

They represented to the president that in view of the fact that Canadian goods could not go through American ports without being subject to this duty on the other side, the United States government should compel all goods coming through Canada in bond and bound for the United States to pay a ten per cent duty. Let me give one instance of the effect that would have if by any means the United States decided to do that. Take, for instance, the silk trade. Train loads of silk which have entered Vancouver from Japan travel mostly across Canadian territory on their way to New York. It would mean that we should lose all that business if our government did not take action to make a satisfactory trade arrangement with the United States. That is what might happen.
I hold in my hand an interview which was given by the United States Secretary of State, Mr. Cordell Hull, to the Montreal Star, and which appeared in its issue of the seventeenth instant. The interview says:
Then the secretary launched into a general discussion of world trade in which he declared emphatically that any special agreements between nations or groups of nations, large or small, cause the total volume of world trade to drop, however much they may increase business between the particular countries concerned.
It continues:
In one part of the discussion. Secretary Hull as much as admitted that this nationalistic trend is a movement in the wrong direction when he said that the people of the United States are turning towards greater foreign trade as a way out of the depression, adding that "they have tried everything else and it lias failed."
There is no question, sir, that in the last number of years, and I think this is perhaps one of the reasons why we in this country have not been able to make a reciprocal trade arrangement with the United States, the government of that country under President Hoover and President Coolidge were in favour of very high tariffs for their own country and so stated. They felt that their resources were so great in the United States that they did not have to bother with any other country, and that they could live within themselves. I shall never forget listening to President Hoover's addresses over the radio during the 1928 election when he promised the farmers higher protection, and the fishermen higher protection, and the lumbermen and the manufacturers and everyone else. But Mr. Hoover woke up to find that his policy was wrong, and I believe in my soul that the United States to-day realizes that the policy of high protection will not get them anywhere and that they are willing, as Mr. Cordell Hull says in this interview, to make a fair trade arrangement with any other country in the world. He says further:
The world has been twelve years getting into its present difficulties, and it must be several more years getting out. At present we cannot find any considerable number of statesmen in the world who admit and are ready to meet the actualities.
They don't realize that any special agreements for preference rights between any particular countries, no matter how much they increase trade between those nations, decrease the total of world trade. But our own people are growing to recognize this. They have tried everything else and it has failed.
That is my own humble opinion, Mr. Speaker. We should not have these restrictions upon trade and tariffs especially against a great country like the United States where if we had a reciprocal arrangement we would have most to gain by dealing with them. I also feel that their market is so great that they can take everything that we want to sell to them on a fair basis, and consequently I say that this government and this parliament should do everything possible to make a satisfactory trade arrangement with that great country.
The other day when another subject was under discussion in this house, it was mentioned that due to certain conditions in this country there were certain agricultural products higher in price in Canada than in the United States to-day. Of course, that may happen in any country, but why has it happened in Canada? In my opinion the reason there are a few articles higher in price in Canada to-day than in the United States is

all there is a great difference between the hon. gentleman's advocacy to-night and what it was some time ago. He might be good enough to explain how, after his distinguished leader had laboured so sedulously to bring about an agreement with the United States, at the end of nine years the tariff that was then high had been raised twice as high as it was when he came into power, and that notwithstanding the fact that the League of Nations reported, as was admitted in this house, that this is one country on the globe that twice reduced its tariffs.

And there has been no
change in the tariff since. On the first day of May last it was my privilege in this house to read a communication that had been agreed to between the President of the United States and myself. The last paragraph of that communication reads:
We have also discussed the problems peculiar to the United States and Canada. We have agreed to begin a search for means to increase the exchange of commodities between our two countries, and thereby promote not only economic betterment on the North American continent, but also the general improvement of world conditions.
In July the world economic conference met, and on the last day, namely, the fourteenth of July, the Hon. Mr. Cordell Hull, Secretary of State of the United States, who was the ranking head of the delegation from that country at the conference, laid upon the table the following communication:
Although the chief portion of its work is uncompleted, the conference is about to enter upon a recess. During and following this recess, it is hoped that the interested' governments will bring forward, through diplomatic or other channels, substantial proposals aimed to carry out ultimately the fundamental purpose for which the conference was called. I herewith forward a document which I hope will, along with others of a similar character that may come from other sources, receive the attention of those who have the duty of planning the continuation of the work of the conference.
This document contains the outline of a possible agreement for a protracted truce against measures restrictive of international trade. I contemplate that this truce agreement might be carried into effect when and as the conference truce-which, I understand, remains in effect among the adhering states during the recess-may end. This further truce may carry through the longer period required for the carrying out of the general aim of reducing existing barriers. The terms suggested are more precise than those of the conference truce. Other governments may quite
742	COMMONS
Trade with United States-Mr. Bennett
possibly feel that their national necessities would require them to add various points even to the substantial list of reservations and exceptions proposed. A continuing truce should serve to restrict new barriers to such instances of evident and unusual necessity as may arise, even while general governmental policy was aimed in the other direction.
It will be seen that in this document the American government indicates the precise test of necessity which it expects to observe before introducing any new restrictions that may seem imperative for the success of the domestic program of recovery upon which it is engaged. American policy will in general seek to further international commerce to the fullest possible extent compatible with the essential aims of this program.
The document advocates, furthermore, the immediate undertaking of reductions of the existing barriers by the encouragement of bilateral and of practical multilateral agreements. It does not attempt to put into legal form of agreement the terms of possible action; the difficulties of this require further discussion among governments.
lint it does attempt to limit with some degree of precision the exceptions and reservations which may be necessary.
It also sets forth the present American attitude towards other matters involved in commercial treaty negotiations, such as the most favoured nation principle and the possible special exceptions from that principle that might be allowed by governments to facilitate agreements for the lowering of trade barriers
I trust that these proposals will turn out to be a useful contribution to the long term plan of attack upon existing trade obstacles. Despite their limitations and imperfections, I am confident that their acceptance in substance would mark an important advance towards the restoration of international commerce.
The American government reserves the liberty in the course of any future discussion that may take place of modifying its attitude on details. Other governments will no doubt find that their approach to this question, as dictated by their own national situations, is somewhat different and may have modifications and additions to present. However, it is my hope that the governments will be able to adjust their national interests and necessities and devise means for achieving the general purpose upon which we have all agreed.
The sub-appendix which is to be found on page 52 of the printed document which I laid on the table the other day, contains the following:
American suggestion for the further development, during the recess and later stages of the conference, of a program on commercial policy.
Section 1. Are resolved, as a first step in carrying out this program, to endeavour to reach agreement, at the earliest moment favourable to such action, along the following lines.
Then follows a statement of what is to be agreed upon:
The participating governments agree not to introduce any new obstacles, direct or indirect, to the movements of international commerce, whether such obstacles are embodied in new

legislation or brought into existence by the exercise of administrative or executive power under existing legislation. The truce against new barriers is to become effective as between the countries participating in it but will not, subject to treaty obligations, bind participating governments towards those governments which do not participate.
Then follow exceptions (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f), to which the preceding agreement shall be subject. Section 2, however, provides :
Are further resolved forthwith to initiate bilateral or (plurilateral) negotiations for the removal of prohibitions and restrictions and for reduction of tariff rates; and they declare that their aim in these treaties is substantial reduction of basic trade barriers, and not merely the removal of temporary and abnormal restrictions and increments imposed for bargaining purposes.
In shaping its policy and in executing its obligations under any agreements, each government should direct its first and greatest efforts towards eliminating restrictions and reducing duties which most clearly lack economic justification, particularly:
(a)	Duties or restrictions which now completely or almost completely exclude foreign competition, such as those which restrict importation of particular commodities to less than five per cent of the domestic consumption ther-of;
(b)	Duties or restrictions on articles the imports of which have' been substantially curtailed since 1929 as compared with domestic consumption;
(c)	Protective duties or restrictions which have been in effect a considerable period of time without bringing about a substantial domestic production of the protected commodities (say equal to 15 per cent of the total domestic consumption thereof).
Without following that in detail, as my time is limited, I desire to point out that in the language which was used in this house in the document which was communicated to the United States after my visit to Washington, we did not use idle phrases. In the nine months which have elapsed since that statement was made, informal conversations with Washington have been continued and several methods of improving trade relations between Canada and the United States have been carefully examined. I need hardly refer to what took place when the prohibition amendment of the United States was eliminated by popular action. One difficulty has been that President Roosevelt did not secure from congress at the special session which ended last June, new tariff bargaining machinery to facilitate the negotiation of trade agreements with foreign countries. At the time of my visit the early enactment of this legislation was expected. There are indications that legislation looking to the creation of that machinery will be sought at the present session

Trade with United States-Mr. Bennett
of congress and, if it is enacted, I hope negotiations for a trade agreement with Canada will be undertaken forthwith. Alternative means of improving tirade under the existing procedure have also been under consideration. This government is ready to accept any reasonable opportunity which may offer of trade on an equitable basis.
Further, it is a matter of common knowledge that the progress of President Roosevelt's domestic policies for the development of industry and agriculture have caused him to postpone the working out of his plan for the stimulation of international trade by trade agreements. Therefore, having regard to present conditions, having regard to what has taken place during the past nine months, having regard to the action now pending in the congress of the United States and having regard to what took place at the world economic conference and the attitude of the United States as dictated by the Secretary of State of that country, I move, seconded by the Minister Finance (Mr. Rhodes):
That all the words after the word "that" in the said resolution be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

"on the 1st day of May, 1933, the Prime Minister informed this house that the governments of Canada and the United States of America had agreed to begin a search for means to increase the exchange of commodities between the two countries and thereby promote not only economic betterment on the North American continent but also the general improvement of world conditions, and while no trade agreement between the two countries has yet been arrived at, this house approves of the government continuing their efforts to that end."
That amendment embodies a record of the situation since my visit to Washington in 1933 and carries transactions down to the present moment, including the discussion, which I have not amplified to-night because of lack of time, of what took place at the world economic conference. I suggest to hon. members that it might be well to read the conditions which Mr. Secretary Hull indicated should be laid down in the making of any trade agreement. I can only add that any trade agreement that is arrived at between the United States and Canada must be based upon a fair and equitable understanding of conditions in one country by the other, and might I remind the hon. gentleman who has moved this resolution (Mr. Duff) that this is the parliament of Canada and not the congress of the United States of America.

Judging from what he has said and the way in which he has said it, one
would think he was merely indicating to this chamber that this parliament for some reasons unknown had prevented the United States from buying its requirements from Canada. In view of what took place under my predecessor and his efforts to negotiate a lower tariff trade agreement with the United States and of what has taken place since this government came into power, I can only once more remind this chamber that this is the parliament of Canada and not the congress of the United States; that the congress of the United States has to do with its tariffs and its duties, and the parliament of Canada, although the hon. gentleman has spoken as he has with respect to the causes that brought about the creation of two countries, has not yet the authority or power to legislate on tariff matters for the United States of America.
